title: Your AI agents hold credentials — do you know what they can reach?
author: Netability Singapore
tags: AI Risk · Cybersecurity · Zero Trust · Ai agent
body:
For two years the question about AI was what a model might say. That question has moved on. Agents now act — reading mail, querying systems, calling APIs, making changes. They hold credentials. The risk is no longer a bad answer; it is an unauthorised action taken at machine speed.

The attack that exploits this is indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden inside something the agent reads rather than something a user types. A line buried in a supplier invoice, a support ticket, a web page the agent was asked to summarise. Nobody sees it. The agent follows it, using whatever access it was given. Security researchers now report these indirect attacks as the majority of prompt injection incidents, and as materially more successful than the direct kind.

Gartner's warning this year is worth repeating: applying uniform governance across every agent, regardless of its autonomy and scope, is itself a cause of failure. What matters is the distinction between what an agent is able to do and how far its access reaches. Gartner also expects more than four in ten agentic projects to be abandoned — often because autonomy was granted before anyone defined the boundaries.

The gap we see most often is simple. Agents get deployed without identities. No named service account, no least-privilege scoping, no audit trail of what the agent did and on whose behalf. The controls any firm would insist on for a human administrator go unapplied to a process that works faster and never pauses.

For Singapore firms, MAS's Guidelines on AI Risk Management are still in consultation, but the proposed text covers autonomous agents explicitly, and MAS has already published an AI Risk Management Operationalisation Handbook with 24 banks, insurers and capital markets firms through Project MindForge. There is enough direction to act on now.

Three things worth doing before a pilot becomes production: give every agent its own identity, scope its access to the minimum it genuinely needs, and log its actions somewhere you will actually review. None of that waits on the guidelines being finalised.

We help firms in Singapore apply the identity, segmentation and monitoring controls that make agent deployments defensible. If you are piloting agents, it is worth knowing what they can reach.

title: Nagios Fusion 2026R2: rebuilt interface, live event collection and role-based access
author: Netability Singapore
body:
Nagios has released Fusion 2026R2, and it is the most substantial change to the product in years — a full rebuild on Laravel and React, with a redesigned interface, new dashboards and a role-based permission system.

Fusion is the single pane of glass across a Nagios estate. It brings Nagios XI, Nagios Log Server and Nagios Network Analyzer together so system, network and log problems surface in one place, instead of logging into each server in turn to piece a picture together.

Three things stand out in this release.

**A rebuilt interface.** Fusion now runs on modern frameworks, and it shows in how quickly dashboards load and respond. Dashlets are drag and drop, so each team can assemble the view it actually needs rather than living with a fixed layout.

**Event-based collection.** Fusion takes live alerts and updates directly from XI, Log Server and Network Analyzer, so the console reflects what is happening as it happens rather than at the next polling interval.

**Role-based permissions.** User roles let you grant or restrict visibility per user and per fused server.

That last point carries more weight than it first appears. For firms operating under MAS TRM expectations, demonstrating least-privilege access and segregation of duties across your monitoring platform is exactly the kind of control that comes up in a review — and a monitoring console that aggregates every environment you run is not a small thing to hand out blanket access to.

We design, deploy and support Nagios across Singapore, including custom check scripts, event handlers and alert tuning. If you are already running Fusion, we can advise on the upgrade path and what the rebuild means for any customisation you depend on. If you are running several Nagios servers without Fusion, this release is a good moment to look at consolidating them.

title: MAS AI risk guidelines are coming - The work to start now is your AI inventory
author: Netability Singapore
tags: MAS Compliance, AI Risk, Technology Risk
cta_text: Talk to us about AI risk
body:
MAS issued its consultation paper on Guidelines for AI Risk Management in November 2025. The consultation closed on 31 January 2026, and this month MAS Chairman and Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said the Guidelines will be finalised soon.

When they are issued, financial institutions get a proposed twelve-month transition period. That sounds generous. For most firms it won't be.

The Guidelines apply to every MAS-regulated financial institution and cover four areas: AI governance and oversight, risk management systems and processes, controls across the AI lifecycle, and the capability to run all of it. Boards and senior management are given explicit responsibilities — setting risk appetite, approving frameworks, and holding enough AI literacy to meaningfully challenge what they approve.

The requirement that takes longest is the simplest to state: maintain an accurate, current inventory of where AI is used across your organisation, with a structured assessment of how material each use is.

Most firms underestimate this. AI is already in your environment whether you procured it deliberately or not — Copilot across Microsoft 365, AI features switched on by default in SaaS you already licence, models embedded inside vendor products. An inventory that captures only the AI projects you formally approved will not survive scrutiny.

The transition clock hasn't started yet. That is precisely why this is the moment to build the inventory — while it's preparation rather than remediation.

title: New service: continuous MAS Cyber Hygiene scoring and board reporting
author: Netability Singapore
tags: MAS Compliance, Cybersecurity, Cyber Hygiene, CMS
body:
We've launched a dedicated MAS Cyber Hygiene service for financial institutions in Singapore — continuous assessment across all six domains of the Notice, with scored reports ready for management and board review at any time.

The Notice on Cyber Hygiene sets binding requirements in six areas:

- **Administrative accounts** — securing every privileged account across systems, databases and network devices
- **Security patches** — applying available patches to address vulnerabilities in a timely manner
- **Security standards** — establishing and enforcing a baseline security standard
- **Network perimeter defence** — restricting unauthorised traffic at the perimeter
- **Malware protection** — deploying anti-malware measures on every system where available
- **Multi-factor authentication** — MFA on all administrative accounts for critical systems, and on internet-facing accounts that reach customer information

Most institutions we speak to can demonstrate compliance on the day of an assessment. Far fewer can show it held every day in between — and that gap is what surfaces during a review.

Our service maps your environment against each of the six domains, scores your posture continuously rather than annually, and produces the evidence in a format your board and your regulator both accept. Where gaps appear, we remediate them with the same engineers who found them.

If you're a bank, insurer, capital markets or payment services licensee, this applies to you. Talk to us for a scoping review.

title: SSL/TLS certificates are getting shorter — here's the timeline to 47 days
author: Netability Singapore
cta_text: Talk to us about certificate automation
body:
The industry is phasing out long-lived SSL/TLS certificates. Following CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-081v3 — approved in April 2025 — the maximum validity of a public certificate drops from 398 days today to just 47 days by 2029.

Here's the schedule every organisation should plan around:

- Today — 398 days maximum validity
- 15 March 2026 — 200 days maximum validity
- 15 March 2027 — 100 days maximum validity
- 15 March 2029 — 47 days maximum validity

Domain validation reuse windows shrink in step, reaching just 10 days in 2029. In practice, manually renewing certificates once a year will no longer be viable — teams that don't automate face far more frequent renewals and a real risk of costly outages from expired certificates.

The changes apply to publicly-trusted certificates in the Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge trust stores. Internal PKIs are not affected.

Netability helps organisations get ahead of this shift with automated certificate lifecycle management — discovery, issuance, renewal and monitoring — so expiries never take a service down. Talk to us before the first deadline in March 2026.

title: MAS FAA-N16 voice recording amendments: what financial advisers must do before the deadline
author: Netability Singapore
author_title: IT Cyber Security, Cloud & MAS Compliance
cta_text: Learn about our voice recording solution
body:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore amended Notice FAA-N16 on 29 December 2025, tightening requirements for the recording and retention of client communications. Licensed and exempt financial advisers now face clearer obligations around mobile call capture and audit trails.

Our compliance team has broken down the practical steps — from Tier 1 mobile recording to Microsoft Teams capture — to help your firm stay ahead of the requirements.

title: Why network microsegmentation stops ransomware where firewalls can't
author: Netability Singapore
author_title: IT Cyber Security, Cloud & MAS Compliance
body:
Traditional perimeter security assumes threats come from outside. But once an attacker is inside your network, a flat network lets them move laterally to critical systems within minutes.

We've partnered with Zero Networks to deploy automated, identity-based microsegmentation — isolating every device so a breach in one place can't spread. Deployment takes days, not months.

- Automatic policy generation from observed traffic
- Identity-based access control, MFA-enforced
- No agents, no network redesign
